units.title: Mild to Moderate Hypertension: Classification and the Age-based Table
units.sec: Mild to Moderate Hypertension: Classification and the Age-based Table · p89
units.guide: Antihypertensives are first classified by prescribing preference: first-line drugs are ACE inhibitors/ARBs, long-acting calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) and thiazide diuretics (chlorthalidone), while second-line drugs are alpha blockers, beta blockers, the alpha-2 agonist clonidine, direct renin inhibitors (aliskiren) and spironolactone. The age-based table then explains the renin logic: young hypertensives are hyperreninemic and respond to ACE inhibitors/ARBs, whereas old hypertensives are hyporeninemic and respond to calcium channel blockers.

units.title: Clinical Approach: Newly Diagnosed Hypertension and Resistant Hypertension
units.sec: Clinical Approach: Newly Diagnosed Hypertension and Resistant Hypertension · p89
units.guide: In a newly diagnosed hypertensive without comorbidities, the choice follows age: below 55 years start ACE inhibitors/ARBs (they lower renin), above 55 years start calcium channel blockers (no effect on renin). If there is no response despite maximum dose after one month, combine A + C; if still no response after another month add the third first-line drug to make A + C + D. Resistance to three drugs of which one is a diuretic defines resistant hypertension, which is treated by adding spironolactone to counteract the raised aldosterone.

units.title: Hypertension with Comorbidities
units.guide: The comorbidity flowchart picks the drug by the associated disease: ACE inhibitors/ARBs for diabetes mellitus, CKD without edema, nephrotic syndrome and scleroderma; thiazides for CKD with edema, osteoporosis and renal insufficiency (metolazone being specific); alpha blockers (prazosin) for BPH; calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) for Raynaud disease and cyclosporine-induced HTN; and beta blockers for migraine, essential tremor, anxiety disorders, hyperthyroidism and stable angina.

units.title: Severe Hypertension: Emergency versus Urgency
units.sec: Severe Hypertension: Emergency versus Urgency · p90
units.guide: Severe hypertension means uncontrolled blood pressure of 220/135 mmHg or more, and the next step is to assess for signs of end-organ damage. If end-organ damage is present it is a hypertensive emergency treated with IV drugs (hydralazine, enalaprilat, furosemide, labetalol as DOC in pregnancy, esmolol, nitroglycerine, nitroprusside and dihydropyridines); if end-organ damage is absent it is a hypertensive urgency treated with oral drugs (clonidine as DOC, captopril and nifedipine). End-organ damage signs are encephalopathy, retinopathy, CHF, pulmonary edema, renal failure and eclampsia.
